sysd-blocks-093.title: Normalization: storing each fact in one place
sysd-blocks-093.text:
Store every fact in exactly one place, and a whole class of inconsistencies cannot happen. That is the promise of database normalization: structuring a relational database by formal rules, to cut down repeated data and improve the integrity of what is stored. Edgar F. Codd first proposed it as part of his relational model. The rules are applied in one of two ways, by synthesis, which creates a new database design, or by decomposition, which improves an existing one. The rules themselves form a ladder (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-095}}).

Normalization organizes a database's columns and tables so that integrity constraints enforce their dependencies properly. The goal is that each elementary fact is recorded in only one place, so insertions, updates and deletions maintain consistency automatically. The benefits are concrete: less repeated data, more consistent data, a better data design and enforced referential integrity. A fully normalized database can also take new types of data with minimal changes to its structure, so the applications that use it are minimally affected.

The costs are just as concrete: a more complex data design, more joins, slower performance and maintenance overhead. Some designs therefore give up part of normalization on purpose (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-107}}).

sysd-blocks-084.title: Database index: faster reads, slower writes
sysd-blocks-084.text:
Without help, finding a row by one of its field values means testing rows one by one. That takes O(N) linear time on average, so the work grows in step with the size of the table. A database index is the help: a data structure that speeds up finding rows, at the cost of extra writes and storage to maintain it.

An index is a copy of selected columns, much like a table of contents. It stores the column's values together with a key or pointer to the whole row, so the complete row can be retrieved efficiently. It can be built on one or more columns, which gives rapid random lookups and efficient ordered access. Many designs reach logarithmic O(log(N)) lookup, and some applications can reach flat O(1) lookup. Either way, the lookup is sub-linear.

The bargain is write speed and storage in exchange for read speed. The index must be updated along with the data, so writes slow down, and designs balance lookup speed, index size and update cost. Indexes also create different views of the same data, so a large data set can offer different filters or sorting schemes without extra copies. Some databases index values transformed by a function or expression, such as upper(last_name), or build a partial index covering only records that meet a condition. Because many transactions access an index at once, it also needs concurrency control.

sysd-blocks-182.title: Hash table: jumping straight to the value
sysd-blocks-182.text:
A hash table finds a value without searching for it. The key is hashed (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-106}}), and the hash says where the value is stored. In a well-dimensioned table, the average lookup time does not depend on how many elements it holds. Search, insert and delete cost Θ(1) on average, against O(n) in the worst case. Hash tables implement associative arrays, in-memory tables, caches and sets, and Python dictionaries, Java HashMap and Go maps are built on them.

Most hash functions are imperfect, so different keys can get the same index. Those collisions must be handled, typically by separate chaining or open addressing (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-183}}). The load factor, the ratio of stored elements to slots, also matters. Performance deteriorates as it grows, so implementations keep it below a maximum and resize, or rehash, the table when it is reached. Rehashing is simple but expensive, so real-time systems may resize gradually. A hash table can also serve as a disk-based database index, although a tree-based index is more popular there (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-103}}).

sysd-blocks-103.title: B-tree: a search tree that grows wide, not tall
sysd-blocks-103.text:
A B-tree is a search tree that grows wide instead of tall. It is a self-balancing tree that keeps data sorted and allows searches, sequential access, insertions and deletions in logarithmic time. It generalizes the binary search tree by letting nodes have more than two children, which lowers the tree's height and puts the data in fewer separate blocks. Fewer blocks matter most on disk, which has high latency and large blocks, so databases and file systems use B-trees.

In Knuth's definition, a B-tree of order m has at most m children per node. Non-root internal nodes have at least m/2 (rounded up), and all leaves are on the same level. A non-leaf node with k children holds k-1 keys, which act as separation values dividing its subtrees. Search starts at the root and follows, at each level, the child whose key range contains the search value. Because child counts may vary within a range, a B-tree rebalances less often than other self-balancing trees. The price is some wasted space in nodes that are not full.

sysd-blocks-185.title: Write-ahead log: record the change before making it
sysd-blocks-185.text:
Pull the plug in the middle of a transaction and the database still has to come back whole. Write-ahead logging is the family of techniques that makes this possible. Changes are first recorded in an append-only log on stable storage, and only then written to the database. It gives a database atomicity and keeps committed changes safe, two of the ACID guarantees (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-055}}).

The central rule is that changes to data files may be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. Because of that, data pages need not be flushed at every commit. After a crash, changes not yet applied to the data pages are redone from the log, which is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO. The log also cuts disk writes. Only the sequentially written log file must be flushed to commit a transaction, and one fsync of it may commit many concurrent small transactions. Archiving the log allows recovery to a chosen moment: restore an earlier physical copy, then replay the log to the desired time.

sysd-blocks-111.title: Storage engine: where the database meets permanent storage
sysd-blocks-111.text:
When you save a row, something has to decide how its bytes reach permanent storage. That something is the storage engine, the part of the database engine responsible for putting data into permanent storage. It uses low-level storage structures to serialize the data model, so the data can be written to the chosen medium, and techniques such as indexing may improve performance. In storage, data sits in structures that look completely different from the conceptual level, arranged to make reconstructing it quick when users and programs need it.

A DBMS usually reaches storage through the operating system and its file systems. Storage properties and settings are extremely important for efficient operation, so administrators maintain them closely. Conventional storage is row-oriented, but column-oriented databases also exist. For indexing, the B-tree is the most widely used structure in almost all relational databases. LSM-trees (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-108}}) are widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB.

sysd-blocks-186.title: Inverted index: from words to the documents that hold them
sysd-blocks-186.text:
Reading every word of every document to answer one query is often not technically realistic. An inverted index avoids it: a database index that maps content, such as words, to its locations in a table or in a document or set of documents. It is the most popular data structure in document retrieval systems and a central component of search engines.

Start with a forward index, which stores the list of words per document. Invert it and you get the list of documents per word. With that list, a query jumps to the word by random access, finds the matching documents quickly and then ranks them by relevance. The price is more processing whenever a document is added.

A basic Boolean index records only whether a word occurs in a document, so it finds matches without ranking them. A word-level one also stores each word's positions, which supports phrase search at a cost in processing power and space. PostgreSQL's GIN indexes are inverted indexes with a separate entry for each component value, suited to values such as arrays.

sysd-blocks-187.title: R-tree: indexing places, rectangles and polygons
sysd-blocks-187.text:
Finding every museum within 2 km of a location is the kind of question an R-tree answers. R-trees are tree data structures for spatial access methods, indexing multi-dimensional information such as geographical coordinates, rectangles or polygons, and spatial databases typically prefer them. The key idea is to group nearby objects and represent them by their minimum bounding rectangle one level up. A query that misses a bounding rectangle cannot hit any object inside it.

So search compares each rectangle in a node with the query rectangle and descends only into overlapping children. Most nodes are never read, and at the leaves the stored objects are tested precisely. Like a B-tree, an R-tree is balanced, organizes data in pages and is designed for disk storage. Insertion descends into the subtree needing least enlargement of its bounding box, and a full node is split by a heuristic. The difficulty is a tree that stays balanced while its rectangles neither cover much empty space nor overlap much. R-trees give no worst-case guarantee, but they perform well on real-world data.

sysd-blocks-094.title: Anomalies: how an unnormalized table goes wrong
sysd-blocks-094.text:
Hire a faculty member who has no course yet. A badly designed table may have no place to record them, unless the Course Code is set to null. That is an insertion anomaly, one of three undesirable side effects that can arise when a relation, the formal name for a table, has not been sufficiently normalized.

An update anomaly appears when the same information sits on several rows. Change an address on some skill records only, and the relation is left inconsistent. A deletion anomaly appears when deleting data for one fact forces deleting a different fact. Remove a faculty member's last course record, and the faculty member is lost with it.

Codd's objectives for normalization (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-093}}) included freeing relations from these insertion, update and deletion dependencies and reducing the need to restructure as new data types are introduced. Most relations in third normal form (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-095}}) are free of all three anomalies.

sysd-blocks-104.title: B-trees and disk reads: why wide nodes win
sysd-blocks-104.text:
At about 10 milliseconds per read, finding one record among a million takes 20 disk reads, or 0.2 seconds. A disk read costs far more than comparing keys, thanks to seek time and rotational delay. The fix is to index the index. An auxiliary index holds the first record of each disk block and is about 1% of the size of the original database. Searching it tells which one block to read. Index that index again and it has only 100 entries, small enough to fit in one disk block. Three block reads then replace 14, and the record takes 30 milliseconds instead of 150.

This hierarchy of blocks, from a root block down to the leaf level, is the core idea behind the B-tree. Search cost falls from roughly log2 N disk reads to logb N, where b is the blocking factor: with 100 entries per block, log100 1,000,000 is 3 reads. When an index is searched often, its upper levels may sit in a disk cache and cost no disk read at all.

sysd-blocks-105.title: B+ tree and B* tree: two refinements of the B-tree
sysd-blocks-105.text:
Db2, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite all index their tables with a variant of the B-tree called the B+ tree. A B+ tree can be viewed as a B-tree whose nodes hold only keys, not key-value pairs, with an added bottom level of linked leaves.

Internal nodes hold no record pointers, so every record pointer sits in a leaf. The result is a high fanout, meaning many children per node, typically 100 or more. That makes the tree shallow and cuts the I/O operations needed to find an element. Leaves are often linked in a list, which makes range queries and ordered iteration simpler and more efficient. A B-tree cannot build such a list, since not all its keys are in the leaves.

The B* tree is a different refinement. It keeps non-root nodes at least 2/3 full instead of 1/2. It postpones costly node splits by sharing keys with a neighboring node, a spill that needs no new node.

sysd-blocks-085.title: Clustered and non-clustered indexes: where the rows live
sysd-blocks-085.text:
A table's rows can sit on disk in only one order, so a table can have only one clustered index. A clustered index stores the rows in the order of the index key, while a non-clustered index is a separate sorted structure that points to rows stored elsewhere.

Clustering helps mainly when data is read sequentially in index order or as a range, because neighboring rows are adjacent and fewer data block reads are needed. A non-clustered index keeps its keys in sorted order, and its leaf level points to each record, so the physical row order differs from the index order. A table can have many of them, usually on non-primary-key columns used in JOIN, WHERE and ORDER BY clauses. The difference shows in the leaf. In Microsoft SQL Server, the leaf node of a clustered index is the actual data, not a pointer to data stored elsewhere as in a non-clustered index.

sysd-blocks-108.title: Log-structured merge-tree: built for a flood of writes
sysd-blocks-108.text:
Writing data sequentially is cheaper than scattering it in separate random access requests, and the log-structured merge-tree, or LSM tree, is built on that fact. It suits indexed access to files with a high insert volume, such as transactional log data. It keeps key-value pairs in two or more separate structures, each optimized for its storage medium.

In a two-level LSM tree, a smaller component, C0, lives entirely in memory and C1 lives on disk. New records go into C0, and when it exceeds a size threshold, a contiguous segment of it is merged into C1. Sequential writing cuts total seek time on hard disks and latency on solid-state storage.

LSM trees were designed for write-intensive workloads. When reads and writes mix, compaction, the merging of segments, invalidates cached data in buffer caches, and reads can see high latency and low throughput. Cassandra uses an LSM tree index to optimize write throughput, in contrast to the B-tree indexes most databases use.

sysd-blocks-107.title: Denormalization: trading redundancy for read speed
sysd-blocks-107.text:
Normalizing a database spreads its facts across many tables, and reading them back takes joins. Across several relations stored as separate files, a join can be slow, even prohibitively so. Denormalization is the strategy applied to a previously normalized database to increase performance, by adding redundant copies of data or grouping data. It improves read performance at the expense of some write performance, often to cope with very large numbers of reads.

There are two strategies. The DBMS can store and keep consistent the redundant copies, as with indexed or materialized views, or the designer can denormalize the logical design by hand. A hand-made design can match the query speed. But the designer must keep the copies consistent with constraints that slow writes, so under heavy write load it may perform worse than the normalized design. Denormalization should come only after a satisfactory level of normalization, such as third normal form. The gains are faster retrieval and easier queries; the costs are expensive inserts and updates and a greater chance of inconsistent data.

sysd-blocks-183.title: Hash collision resolution: chaining or probing
sysd-blocks-183.text: Two keys that hash to the same index must both still be found. Separate chaining builds a linked list of key-value pairs for each array index and traverses the list during a lookup. Open addressing stores every entry in the bucket array itself. It probes from the hashed-to slot, by linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing, until it finds an empty slot. Open addressing degrades sharply as its load factor nears 1, with a maximum of about 0.6 to 0.75. Chaining degrades gradually, with the best maximum typically between 1 and 3. Cuckoo hashing guarantees O(1) worst-case lookup.

sysd-blocks-099.title: B-tree versus LSM-tree: faster reads or faster writes
sysd-blocks-099.text: The biggest difference between a B-tree and an LSM-tree can be said in one line: a B-tree enables faster reads, while an LSM-tree enables fast writes. The B-tree is the most widely used indexing data structure in almost all relational databases, and its basic unit of storage is usually called a page. A lookup traces down the range of keys until it finds the actual value. LSM-trees are widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB. An LSM-tree keeps key-value pairs and persists them to disk in a Sorted Strings Table (SSTable) with sorted keys. Level 0 segments are periodically merged into level 1 by compaction.

sysd-blocks-090.title: Index data structures: no single best choice
sysd-blocks-090.text:
A database index can be built on several data structures, and the best choice depends on the workload. The format that fits depends on whether data is indexed in memory or on disk, on the data formats, and on whether the system is write-heavy or read-heavy.

A few structures recur. A skiplist (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-184}}) is a common in-memory index type. A hash index is a common implementation of a map, and an SSTable is an immutable on-disk map. Two of the designs built from them differ sharply. An LSM tree combines a skiplist with SSTables for high write throughput, while a B-tree is a disk-based structure with consistent read and write performance. Other structures serve narrower questions. An inverted index serves document indexing, a suffix tree serves string pattern search, and an R-tree serves multi-dimensional search such as finding the nearest neighbor. Among the popular implementations are balanced trees, B+ trees and hashes.

sysd-blocks-188.title: PostgreSQL index types and what each is for
sysd-blocks-188.text: CREATE INDEX makes a B-tree by default, which fits the most common situations. The USING keyword picks another of PostgreSQL's types: Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN, plus the bloom extension. B-trees handle equality and range queries on sortable data and serve prefix patterns such as LIKE 'foo%', but not LIKE '%bar'. Hash indexes handle only equality. GiST covers geometric types and nearest-neighbor searches, and SP-GiST supports non-balanced structures such as quadtrees and tries. GIN indexes are inverted indexes for values with several components, such as arrays. BRIN indexes summarize block ranges by minimum and maximum, so they suit columns that correlate with physical row order.
